title: Pine Valley Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Pine Valley wells have a 318-foot median depth, with fractured mountain bedrock affecting yield, siting, and drilling cost.
h1: Pine Valley, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a house in Pine Valley means understanding the local well record before you rely on a driller’s estimate. Permitted wells within 5 miles show a median depth of 318 feet, a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 96 feet below ground.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That fits the mountain setting, where granite and gneiss can produce very different results from one lot to the next. Use nearby well records as a starting point, then have a licensed contractor evaluate the actual homesite, access, septic layout, and water supply.

sections.heading: Pine Valley wells usually reach fractured mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The local depth record points to substantial drilling. The median completed depth is 318 feet, while the middle half of reported wells falls from 200 to 485 feet. That middle range is the most useful starting point for a bid, but it is not a guarantee for a particular parcel.

About 42% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet, and 15% exceed 600 feet. Another 34% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 9% are under 100 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 3,523 feet. Permits most often name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with fractured crystalline and fractured granite also appearing.

sections.heading: A 7-gpm median is a workable local benchmark
sections.html:
Reported well yields have a median of 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 4.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. For a typical household, that range can be a reasonable production target, but storage and well recovery still matter. A yield test is more useful than a regional average when you are evaluating a specific property.

The records show 62% of reported wells producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 27% produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 2% are under 1 gallon per minute and 9% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Fractured rock can change abruptly across short distances, so neighboring results are evidence, not a promise.

sections.heading: Water levels look deeper than the earliest records
sections.html:
Among wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 96 feet, with the middle half from 50 to 150 feet below the surface. That measurement describes the water level when the well is not being pumped; it is not the same as well depth or pumping yield.

The decade series moves from 29 feet in the 1960s to 68 feet in the 1970s and 95 feet in the 1980s. It was 82 feet in the 1990s, then 100 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. The available record suggests deeper water levels than in the earliest measurements, but the dataset includes only 174 static-water reports, so it should not be treated as a complete groundwater trend for every lot.

sections.heading: Permit activity spans Pine Valley and nearby mountain corridors
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 4,779 permitted wells within the five-mile study area. Of those, 3,128 are recorded as constructed, 3,229 report a total depth, and 1,685 report a pump yield. The permits are overwhelmingly domestic or household use at 94%; stock, irrigation, and monitoring uses make up the remainder.

Activity was strongest in the 1970s, with 1,128 permits, and the 1990s, with 1,088. The newest permit year is 2025. The most frequent driller names in the records are James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.), Walton, and Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert). Compare records around Echo Hills, Upper Witter Gulch, Floyd Hill, Blue Valley, and Upper Bear Creek before choosing a contractor.

sections.heading: Budget roughly $26,700 to $43,800 for a finished median-depth well
sections.html:
In Pine Valley’s fractured granite and gneiss, the drilling rate model is $65 to $100 per foot. Applied to the 318-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models at about $20,700 to $31,800.

A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, models at about $26,700 to $43,800 at that depth. Treat this as a planning range, not a fixed quote. Access, casing and grout requirements, difficult ground, water storage, power distance, and the final well depth can move the total. Ask every bidder to separate drilling from completion, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and any work needed to reach the homesite.

sections.heading: Mine features and septic layout deserve a close review
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only local concern. The mapping shows 27 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2,207 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These mapped sites do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to check the well’s construction record, test existing water, and review nearby land uses before closing.

Have the well water tested for ordinary household quality and for site-specific concerns identified in the area review. Confirm that the proposed well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and house can fit on the lot with required separations. A low-producing or dry hole can also leave a parcel without a practical household supply. A DWR permit, casing, grout, and a properly documented completion matter for both construction and resale.

sections.heading: Check the records before you buy or start a build
sections.html:
Start with the closest permitted wells, especially in Echo Hills, Upper Witter Gulch, Floyd Hill, Blue Valley, and Upper Bear Creek. Compare their depths, reported yields, static water levels, aquifer descriptions, and dates. A nearby 318-foot well with a 7.0-gpm yield is useful context, but fractured rock can change quickly between lots.

For an existing home, request the well permit, construction report, pump information, recent water test, and a current production or recovery evaluation. For vacant land, confirm access for a rig, estimate a drilling range around the local 200- to 485-foot middle half, and design the septic and house locations before drilling. Also ask how the proposed use fits the permit. Household-use exempt wells are common in Colorado, but pumping, augmentation, and land-use requirements depend on the permit and basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Pine Valley, Colorado?
faq.a: Pine Valley wells have a median reported depth of 318 feet. The middle half runs from 200 to 485 feet, while 42% fall between 300 and 600 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make individual results unpredictable, so nearby permits are useful for estimating a lot but cannot guarantee its final depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Pine Valley?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 318-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $20,700 to $31,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is modeled at $26,700 to $43,800. Access and actual depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Pine Valley wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half produces 4.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells, 62%, fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. About 2% are under 1 gallon per minute, so a production test and storage review are important before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Pine Valley?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The area has 27 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2,207 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Test an existing well, review nearby land uses, and check construction records before relying on the water.

faq.q: Who drills wells near Pine Valley, Colorado?
faq.a: The most active driller names in the records are James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.), Walton, and Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert). The records identify past permit activity, not a guarantee of current availability or suitability. Get current bids and compare scope, access assumptions, testing, casing, grout, and completion equipment.
